passages.text: Post-CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy in HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer: expanding options and persisting uncertainties

Endocrine treatment in combination with CDK4/6 inhibitors represents the mainstay of first-line palliative treatment in HR+/HER2- breast cancer. <sentence_start/>The treatment landscape after progression on CDK4/6 inhibitors has evolved into a complex and rapidly evolving field, driven by novel endocrine and targeted agents, new combination therapies, and increasing implementation of biomarker-directed approaches. <sentence_start/>Recent randomized trials have shown that new therapeutic strategies significantly prolong progression-free survival in this setting, with some treatments reaching notable numerical improvements. <sentence_start/>Translating these options into routine clinical practice remains challenging due to heterogeneous trial designs, lack of head-to-head comparisons, suboptimal comparator treatments, and limited overall survival data. <sentence_start/>While the increasing implementation of biomarkers holds the potential for more personalized treatments, their clinical utility depends on their mechanistic and contextual biological relevance, methodological reliability of detection, and proven predictive value in clinical trials. <sentence_start/>Based on the current evidence, optimal treatment selection and sequencing in the post-CDK4/6 inhibitor setting remain insufficiently defined, and optimization of biomarker-guided treatment requires further mechanistic understanding and methodological refinement. <sentence_start/>This narrative review provides an overview of the most recent randomized clinical trial evidence shaping current clinical practice and discusses persistent uncertainties regarding its implementation in routine care.

Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer and remains the leading cause of cancer mortality in females globally [<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41591-025-03502-3" pmid="39994475" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Prognosis and treatment of advanced breast cancer (ABC) depend on the respective subtype, with hormone-receptor positive (HR+), HER2-negative (HER2-) disease representing the most prevalent one [<citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jama.2018.19323" pmid="30667505" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The introduction of CDK4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) in combination with endocrine therapy (ET) has led to substantial therapeutic advances in HR+/HER2- locally advanced inoperable and metastatic breast cancer (here collectively referred to as ABC). <sentence_start/>As a result, these agents have become a mainstay of first-line palliative therapy and have more recently been incorporated into the adjuvant setting [<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.10.005" pmid="41110697" count="1">3</citation>-<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2024.04.013" pmid="38729566" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Despite these advances, the vast majority of patients receiving CDK4/6i therapy in the advanced disease setting inevitably experience disease progression, necessitating subsequent lines of therapy. <sentence_start/>Therapeutic decision-making after progression on CDK4/6i-based first-line therapy, however, remains highly complex. <sentence_start/>An expanding variety of therapeutic options, driven by positive results from recent clinical trials, challenges treating physicians to select the optimal, personalized treatment strategy.

According to current guidelines, treatment after progression on ET in combination with a CDK4/6i should be individualized according to a multifactorial, not clearly standardized, assessment of continued suitability for endocrine-based treatment [<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.07.017" pmid="40930896" count="1">12</citation>-<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In clinical practice, this distinction often reflects a continuum informed by (Figure 1): <italic>i</italic>) urgency for treatment response, including symptomatic or high disease burden and possibly impending organ dysfunction, <italic>ii</italic>) anticipated benefit of another endocrine-based therapy (evaluated by prior treatment history and biomarker profile, amongst others), <italic>iii</italic>) general health condition, comorbidities and preferences of the patient [<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.07.017" pmid="40930896" count="1">12</citation>-<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>].

<bold>Determinants influencing treatment selection after progression on CDK4/6i and approved drug classes available for HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer.</bold> <sentence_start/>ADCs: antibody-drug conjugates; AKTi: AKT inhibitor; ChT: chemotherapy; PI3Ki: phosphoinositide 3-kinase inhibitor; mTORi: mechanistic target of rapamycin inhibitor; PARPi: Poly(ADP-ribose)-polymerase inhibitor; PROTACs: proteolysis-targeting chimeras. <sentence_start/>Icons provided by Apple Keynote.

In patients still considered candidates for endocrine-based therapy, treatment options are based on switching ET, including novel strategies to target the estrogen receptor (ER), which may be administered 1) as monotherapy, or in combination with 2) CDK4/6i after CDK4/6i, 3) inhibitors of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, or 4) increasingly investigated, a combination of the aforementioned agents. <sentence_start/>In patients deemed ineligible for endocrine-based therapy, escalation to chemotherapy or an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) is warranted (Figure 2). <sentence_start/>Across these decisions, biomarker profiles are increasingly integrated to guide treatment selection [<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.07.017" pmid="40930896" count="1">12</citation>-<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>].

<bold>Potential decision framework in advanced HR+/HER2- breast cancer following CDK4/6i progression.</bold> <sentence_start/>The proposed algorithm reflects the authors’ opinion. <sentence_start/>Selection of novel treatment strategies was restricted to options with fully published trial results. <sentence_start/>HER2-null refers to the complete absence of membranous staining, i.e., HER2- status not meeting the criteria for HER2-low or HER2-ultralow [<citation rid="B106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.modpat.2025.100925" pmid="41167529" count="1">106</citation>]. <sentence_start/>CDK4/6i: CDK4/6 inhibitor; ET: endocrine therapy; <italic>gBRCA1/2</italic>: germline <italic>BRCA1/2</italic>; <italic>gPALB2</italic>: germline <italic>PALB2</italic>; HER2-: HER2-negative; HR+: hormone receptor-positive; IHC: immunohistochemistry; ILD: interstitial lung disease; mTOR: mechanistic target of rapamycin; s<italic>BRCA1/2</italic>: somatic <italic>BRCA1/2.</italic> <sentence_start/>Icons provided by Apple Keynote.

The objective of this narrative review is to provide a structured and comprehensive overview of the most recent randomized clinical trial evidence relevant to guide second-line treatment in HR+/HER2- ABC following progression on CDK4/6i therapy. <sentence_start/>We aim to address the heterogeneity and limitations of trial designs regarding patient populations, comparator treatment and endpoints, and discuss the resulting constraints in cross-trial interpretation and translation of results into clinical practice. <sentence_start/>As precision oncology has become a defining feature in this setting, reflected in a one-to-one biomarker-to-treatment matching in both contemporary clinical trial design and clinical practice algorithms, we explore aspects of mechanistic, methodological and clinical uncertainties related to biomarker-guided treatment selection, and discuss aspects of practical guidance within this complexity.

To characterize the current second-line, randomized clinical trial evidence in this narrative review, we conducted a literature search in PubMed using a combination of MeSH terms and free-text terms covering breast cancer, hormone receptor positivity and advanced stage. <sentence_start/>Publications were restricted to randomized phase II and III trials published between January 2016 and March 10, 2026. <sentence_start/>Trial evidence from the literature search reporting positive outcomes was included if it aligned with the scope of this review (defined as treatment options post CDK4/6i progression; studies with a more heavily pretreated population were not considered). <sentence_start/>Negative results were included at the authors’ discretion when they were considered helpful for discussing specific aspects. <sentence_start/>In addition, an exploratory search of PubMed and Google Scholar was performed, and international oncologic guidelines and resources from major oncology congresses were consulted to identify additional trials and complementary and contextual information. <sentence_start/>The summary of trial evidence was restricted to results published (in full or abstract form) until March 10, 2026, whereas contextual information was considered until June 30, 2026.

Unless otherwise stated, presented outcomes derive from fully published peer-reviewed clinical trial evidence; where abstract-only data are cited, this is explicitly noted. <sentence_start/>Subgroup analyses for biomarker-selected patients are reported where they reflect primary or secondary endpoints, or where the trial population was restricted to a biomarker-selected subgroup, unless otherwise stated. <sentence_start/>Exploratory subgroup analyses stratified by CDK4/6i pretreatment were preferentially reported (and explicitly labeled as such), given their relevance to the scope of the review.

The term endocrine resistance carries a context-dependent meaning in second-line treatment of advanced, HR+/HER2- breast cancer. <sentence_start/>A most widely established clinical definition was introduced by the international ABC consensus guidelines, which has since been continuously adapted and which distinguishes between primary and secondary endocrine resistance. <sentence_start/>Primary endocrine resistance has initially been defined as relapse while on the first 2 years of adjuvant ET or progressive disease within the first 6 months of first-line ET in the advanced setting; whereas secondary endocrine resistance has referred to progression on adjuvant ET after the first two years, relapse within 12 months of completing adjuvant ET, or progressive disease ≥ 6 months on ET for ABC [<citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2020.09.010" pmid="32979513" pmcid="PMC7510449" count="1">15</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Those definitions have been updated to include progression on endocrine-based therapies, which also includes CDK4/6i use, and to extend the definition of secondary endocrine resistance to progression on any second-line endocrine-based therapy, and to the presence of <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations [<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.breast.2024.103756" pmid="38896983" pmcid="PMC11231614" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, the distinction between primary and secondary endocrine resistance as such has not primarily been used to guide clinical decision-making for first-line and second-line therapies in the advanced setting, but rather serves to classify patient populations for clinical trials [<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.breast.2024.103756" pmid="38896983" pmcid="PMC11231614" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The recently published ESMO guidelines on metastatic breast cancer (available as pre-proof) also reference these definitions, but do not integrate them into their treatment recommendations. <sentence_start/>At the same time, they introduce the term endocrine-sensitive disease, for which they recommend at least two endocrine-based therapy lines, without clear characterization of the term [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN Guidelines<sup>®</sup>) use the term endocrine-refractory disease to guide treatment decisions, without a precise definition of the term and categorization being based on clinical judgement [<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>].

Mechanistically, endocrine resistance encompasses the cellular and molecular processes by which tumors acquire resistance to ET. <sentence_start/>Endocrine resistance mechanisms have initially been conceptualized in the context of endocrine monotherapy, involving distinct ways by which tumor cells may either reactivate ER signaling despite ET-most prominently exemplified by <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations-or bypass ER signaling via activation of alternative signaling pathways or changes in transcription factors distinct from ER [<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41568-023-00604-3" pmid="37500767" pmcid="PMC10529099" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>With CDK4/6i as a component of first-line and adjuvant therapy, resistance mechanisms under combined ET and CDK4/6i therapy have gained clinical and research interest.

The kinases CDK4 and 6, upon binding cyclin D, phosphorylate the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor protein (Rb), which leads to dissociation of the transcription factor E2F from the Rb/E2F complex and consequently promotes E2F-mediated transcription of genes driving cell cycle progression. <sentence_start/>CDK4/6i inhibit CDK4 and CDK6 kinase activity and Rb phosphorylation, thereby preventing E2F-driven cell cycle progression. <sentence_start/>Mechanisms of resistance to CDK4/6i are numerous, such as functional Rb loss, upregulation of the CDK2-Cyclin E complex (and thereby bypassing CDK4/6 inhibition by alternative Rb phosphorylation), alternative native conformational states of CDK4 and 6, and activation of different growth factor pathways, amongst others [<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41568-023-00604-3" pmid="37500767" pmcid="PMC10529099" count="1">17</citation>, <citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s43018-024-00893-z" pmid="39885369" pmcid="PMC12207747" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>While endocrine resistance remains a widely used term in the second-line setting, it nowadays encompasses resistance to both ET and CDK4/6i, refers to a landscape of resistance mechanisms beyond those induced by ET alone, and lacks a clinically actionable, precise definition. <sentence_start/>In the following, the term endocrine-resistant refers to trial populations with either primary or secondary resistance to ET.

CDK4/6i have evolved as a cornerstone of palliative therapy of HR+/HER2- breast cancer. <sentence_start/>The CDK4/6i abemaciclib, palbociclib, and ribociclib have demonstrated significant improvements in progression-free survival (PFS) when combined with ET in endocrine-naïve, endocrine-pretreated but not resistant, and endocrine-resistant advanced disease [<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2018.78.9909" pmid="29860922" count="1">19</citation>-<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1505270" pmid="26030518" count="1">24</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Abemaciclib added to ET additionally resulted in a clinically meaningful improvement in overall survival (OS), but reached statistical significance only in endocrine-resistant disease [<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamaoncol.2019.4782" pmid="31563959" pmcid="PMC6777264" count="1">5</citation>, <citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2024.04.013" pmid="38729566" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Ribociclib likewise demonstrated an OS benefit in both endocrine-naïve or non-resistant and mixed populations [<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1911149" pmid="31826360" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2114663" pmid="35263519" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Based on the OS benefit observed with adjuvant abemaciclib and the invasive disease-free survival (iDFS) benefit reported with adjuvant ribociclib in high-risk early-stage HR+/HER2- breast cancer, CDK4/6i have expanded into the curative setting [<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.10.005" pmid="41110697" count="1">3</citation>, <citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.esmoop.2025.105858" pmid="41320342" pmcid="PMC12684762" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Treatment options for first-line palliative therapy in patients relapsing during or after adjuvant CDK4/6i resemble those in patients progressing on CDK4/6i in the metastatic setting. <sentence_start/>Potential differences in tumor biology and treatment responses between these groups remain insufficiently explored, and evidence to guide therapy selection in the post-adjuvant-CDK4/6i setting is largely missing. <sentence_start/>In analogy to clinical endocrine resistance mechanisms, suggestions have been made to incorporate definitions of CDK4/6i resistance-including time on or after CDK4/6i prior to recurrence-to inform therapeutic decision-making [<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.esmoop.2025.105758" pmid="40913835" pmcid="PMC12451316" count="1">25</citation>].

The established first-line treatment strategy of ET plus CDK4/6i has been refined following the results of the phase III INAVO120 trial, in which the addition of the PI3K inhibitor inavolisib to palbociclib and fulvestrant improved OS in a <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated, CDK4/6i-naïve population progressing on or shortly after adjuvant ET [<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2501796" pmid="40454641" pmcid="PMC13496148" count="1">26</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interpretation of these results is complicated by the uncertain significance of an OS benefit compared with palbociclib plus fulvestrant, a regimen which itself did not improve OS in this setting [<citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1810527" pmid="30345905" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>With the triplet regimen incorporating CDK4/6i and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway-targeting agents moving into the first-line setting, evidence to guide subsequent treatment is lacking. <sentence_start/>Other first-line strategies under investigation include intensified combination approaches and the earlier use of established second-line or novel therapeutic agents: Ongoing phase III trials evaluating CDK4/6i in the first-line setting in endocrine-sensitive disease (generally allowing for adjuvant CDK4/6i exposure) evaluate triplet regimens with aromatase inhibitor (AI) and the PI3K inhibitor inavolisib [<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.esmoop.2025.104979" count="1">27</citation>], or doublet combinations with novel endocrine agents [<citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2021.39.15_suppl.tps1101" count="1">28</citation>-<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1557-3265.sabcs25-ps5-12-18" count="1">30</citation>], or even challenge the first-line ET plus CDK4/6i approach with the introduction of the more selective CDK4 inhibitor (CDK4i) atirmociclib [<citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.08.1046" count="1">31</citation>]. <sentence_start/>If positive, these trials might change or amend the first-line palliative treatment landscape and will consequently reshape choices for second-line treatment. <sentence_start/>Additionally, in the phase III lidERA trial, results (presented as an abstract) demonstrated that the oral selective ER degrader (SERD) giredestrant showed a benefit in iDFS compared to standard of care (SOC) ET, possibly generating a role of SERD in earlier lines of treatment [<citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1557-3265.sabcs25-gs1-10" count="1">32</citation>].

To date, most patients requiring palliative second-line therapy in HR+/HER2- ABC have received ET in combination with a CDK4/6i. <sentence_start/>In the following, we focus on therapeutic options in this treatment setting, recognizing that further adjustments may be required in the near future.

Inhibition of ER signaling remains the mainstay of palliative therapy in HR+/HER2- breast cancer and can be achieved through estrogen suppression or direct ER targeting, which represents the mechanism of action of several novel agents, including SERDs, proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), selective ER modulators (SERMs) and complete ER antagonists (CERANs) [<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2023.102569" pmid="37146385" count="1">33</citation>].

Mutations in the <italic>ESR1</italic> gene encoding the ER are an acquired resistance mechanism to ET. <sentence_start/><italic>ESR1</italic> mutations induce conformational changes, constitutive activation, and increased proteolytic stability of the ER, thereby inducing resistance to estrogen-depleting approaches with AI, and to a variable extent, different agents directly targeting the ER [<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13058-021-01462-3" pmid="34392831" pmcid="PMC8365900" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic>ESR1</italic> mutations are rare in treatment-naïve HR+/HER2− breast cancer, but occur at a prevalence up to 20-40% in advanced disease treated with AI [<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13058-021-01462-3" pmid="34392831" pmcid="PMC8365900" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>They have been shown to arise during AI therapy, and to precede and correlate with clinical progression [<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13058-020-01290-x" pmid="32466779" pmcid="PMC7254698" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/annonc/mdx483" pmid="29045530" pmcid="PMC6264798" count="1">36</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In contrast to AI, which reduces ER signaling via estrogen deprivation, SERDs inhibit ER-induced downstream signaling by directly binding to the ER and inducing its proteasomal degradation [<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2022.102432" pmid="35839531" pmcid="PMC13394875" count="1">37</citation>].

Fulvestrant had long been the only SERD available for treatment of HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer. <sentence_start/>Following progression on a CDK4/6i, a review of recent randomized phase II-III trials using fulvestrant as control therapy has shown a median PFS of around 3.2 months (range 1.9-5.3 months), consistent with real-world outcomes [<citation rid="B38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers16244179" pmid="39766078" pmcid="PMC11674525" count="1">38</citation>-<citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers17050884" pmid="40075731" pmcid="PMC11898757" count="1">40</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Given the limited clinical activity of fulvestrant after CDK4/6i and its intramuscular route of application due to poor oral bioavailability, oral SERDs were developed to improve potency and enable more convenient oral administration [<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2022.102432" pmid="35839531" pmcid="PMC13394875" count="1">37</citation>].

Elacestrant was the first oral SERD to demonstrate efficacy as monotherapy after mandatory prior CDK4/6i exposure and a maximum of one prior line of chemotherapy in a phase III trial. <sentence_start/>In the EMERALD study, elacestrant was compared with investigator’s choice (IC) of ET (IC ET) (AI or fulvestrant) in patients with disease progression on prior ET plus a CDK4/6i. <sentence_start/>The trial met its two primary endpoints, demonstrating improved PFS in both the overall population and with greater benefit in the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated subgroup (median PFS 3.8 months with elacestrant vs. 1.9 months for IC ET; hazard ratio (HR) 0.55 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.39-0.77]; <italic>P</italic> = 0.0005). <sentence_start/>Landmark analyses demonstrated a 6-month PFS rate of 40.8% with elacestrant vs. 19.1% with IC ET in the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated subgroup. <sentence_start/>A secondary analysis excluded the 31% of patients receiving AIs in the control arm, accounting for the recognized resistance associated with <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations. <sentence_start/>Elacestrant continued to demonstrate benefit over fulvestrant, again with a more pronounced effect in the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated cohort [6-month PFS rate 40.8% vs. 20.8%; HR 0.50 (95% CI 0.34-0.74); <italic>P</italic> = 0.005] [<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.00338" pmid="35584336" pmcid="PMC9553388" count="1">41</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The most common adverse events (AEs) (any grade) with elacestrant were nausea (35%), fatigue (19%), vomiting (19%), decreased appetite (14.8%) and arthralgia (14.3%). <sentence_start/>Among grade ≥ 3 events, nausea (2.5%) and back pain (2.5%) occurred most frequently, followed by increase in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (2.1% and 1.7%, respectively) and headache (1.7%). <sentence_start/>Treatment-related AEs led to treatment discontinuation in 3.4% of patients (Table 1) [<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.00338" pmid="35584336" pmcid="PMC9553388" count="1">41</citation>]. <sentence_start/>No OS benefit was shown at the final OS analysis in either the intention-to-treat (ITT) or the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated population (both key secondary endpoints; 51.3% of the ITT population experienced an event) [<citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.23.02112" pmid="38381994" pmcid="PMC11003513" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A separately published, post-hoc exploratory analysis by pretreatment duration in exclusively <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated patients has been considerably discussed in the field. <sentence_start/>Longer prior CDK4/6i exposure (≥ 12 months) was associated with improved PFS on elacestrant vs. IC ET [8.6 months vs. 1.9 months, HR 0.41 (95% CI 0.26-0.63)] in <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated patients, compared to a shorter pretreatment period [<citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.ccr-24-1073" pmid="39087959" pmcid="PMC11443208" count="1">43</citation>].

The oral SERD camizestrant has likewise shown clinical activity in the randomized phase II SERENA-2 trial, in which two dose levels were compared with fulvestrant following disease progression on ET, with optional prior CDK4/6i and chemotherapy exposure for advanced disease [<citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(24)00387-5" pmid="39481395" count="1">44</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic>ESR1</italic> mutations were detected in 48% of patients in the fulvestrant group and in 30% of those receiving the camizestrant dose [<citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(24)00387-5" pmid="39481395" count="1">44</citation>] that was subsequently selected for further evaluation in the SERENA-4 and 6 trials [<citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2021.39.15_suppl.tps1101" count="1">28</citation>, <citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2502929" pmid="40454637" count="1">45</citation>]. <sentence_start/>At this dose level, camizestrant improved PFS compared with fulvestrant [median PFS 7.2 vs. 3.7 months for camizestrant and fulvestrant, respectively; HR 0.59 (90% CI 0.42-0.82); <italic>P</italic> = 0.017]. <sentence_start/>In the prespecified exploratory analyses by <italic>ESR1</italic> mutation status and prior CDK4/6i exposure (51% of trial population), the relative benefit of camizestrant seemed maintained in patients with <italic>ESR1</italic> mutation [HR 0.33 (90% CI 0.18-0.58)], but not in patients without <italic>ESR1</italic> mutation [HR 0.80 (90% CI 0.51-1.27)]. <sentence_start/>Treatment effect appeared sustained in patients with prior CDK4/6i exposure [HR 0.49 (90% CI 0.31-0.75)], but not without prior CDK4/6i treatment [HR 0.81 (90% CI 0.49-1.33)]. <sentence_start/>Most common treatment-emergent AEs (any grade) with camizestrant 75 mg were photopsia (12%), anemia (10.8%), cough (9.5%), asthenia (8.1%), and nausea (8.1%). <sentence_start/>Treatment-related AEs leading to discontinuation in the camizestrant 75 mg group occurred in 3% of patients. <sentence_start/>No specific treatment-emergent or treatment-related grade ≥ 3 event was observed in > 1 patient (Table 1). <sentence_start/>OS data were immature [<citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(24)00387-5" pmid="39481395" count="1">44</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Camizestrant has been evaluated in combination with a CDK4/6i upon molecular progression in the SERENA-6 trial, as discussed below, and is currently being assessed with palbociclib in the first-line setting in the SERENA-4 trial [<citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2021.39.15_suppl.tps1101" count="1">28</citation>, <citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2502929" pmid="40454637" count="1">45</citation>].

The three-arm phase III EMBER-3 trial compared the oral SERD imlunestrant to IC ET (exemestane or fulvestrant) and to imlunestrant plus abemaciclib. <sentence_start/>Patients were eligible with endocrine-resistant disease after adjuvant or first-line AI therapy, with or without prior CDK4/6i therapy, and no chemotherapy for advanced disease was permitted. <sentence_start/>Ninety percent of patients in the control arm received fulvestrant, and 10% received exemestane [<citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The trial was negative for its primary endpoint PFS with imlunestrant vs. IC ET in the overall population, but a statistically significant PFS benefit [median PFS 5.5 months with imlunestrant and 3.8 months with IC ET; HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.47<italic>-</italic>0.82); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001] in the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated group-another primary endpoint-was demonstrated with initial drop and later separation of the Kaplan-Meier curves [<citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Exploratory subgroup analysis of the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated cohort by prior CDK4/6i therapy showed an HR of 0.42 (95% CI 0.25<italic>-</italic>0.72) in CDK4/6i-naïve and 0.72 (95% CI 0.52<italic>-</italic>1.01) in CDK4/6i-pretreated patients (70% of the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated population, predominantly palbociclib) [<citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A numerical improvement in OS (key secondary endpoint) was observed in favor of imlunestrant without reaching statistical significance in the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated cohort [median OS 34.5 vs. 23.1 months, respectively; HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.43-0.86); <italic>P</italic> = 0.0043, not significant] [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Single-agent ET with imlunestrant was inferior to the combination therapy with abemaciclib, as will be outlined below [<citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The most common AEs of any grade were fatigue/asthenia (22.6%), diarrhea (21.4%), nausea (17.1%), arthralgia (14.1%), and AST increase (12.5%). <sentence_start/>AEs of grade ≥ 3 were anemia and neutropenia (2.1% each), AST increase and thrombopenia (0.9% each) [<citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Treatment-related AEs led to treatment discontinuation in 2% of patients (Table 1) [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>].

The randomized trials evaluating the oral SERDs amcenestrant and giredestrant as monotherapy yielded negative results against IC ET in endocrine-resistant populations with varying degrees of prior CDK4/6i exposure [<citation rid="B48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.02746" pmid="37348019" pmcid="PMC10461947" count="1">48</citation>, <citation rid="B49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO.23.0150" pmid="38537155" pmcid="PMC11185917" count="1">49</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Giredestrant was positive for its primary endpoint, PFS, in the phase III evERA trial in combination with everolimus (full publication results pending), as described below [<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.09.026" count="1">50</citation>], and is currently investigated with a CDK4/6i in phase III trials in the first-line setting in endocrine-sensitive and endocrine-resistant disease [<citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2021.39.15_suppl.tps1103" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="B51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2024.42.16_suppl.tps1130" count="1">51</citation>].

PROTACs represent an additional class of novel endocrine agents with proven clinical efficacy in a phase III trial [<citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2505725" pmid="40454645" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>PROTACs act by recruiting a ubiquitin ligase to a target protein, promoting its polyubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation [<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2023.102569" pmid="37146385" count="1">33</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Vepdegestrant, a first-in-class PROTAC targeting the ER [<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2023.102569" pmid="37146385" count="1">33</citation>], demonstrated superiority over fulvestrant in the phase III VERITAC-2 trial in an endocrine-resistant, post-CDK4/6i population [<citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2505725" pmid="40454645" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Patients had to be on their most recent ET for ≥ 6 months before progression, and no prior chemotherapy or fulvestrant for advanced disease was allowed. <sentence_start/>Vepdegestrant did not meet the primary endpoint of PFS in the ITT population but demonstrated superiority in the primary endpoint of PFS in the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated subgroup [median PFS 5.0 vs. 2.1 months for vepdegestrant and fulvestrant, respectively; HR 0.58 (95% CI 0.43-0.78); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001]. <sentence_start/>Data on OS were immature. <sentence_start/>Most common AEs were fatigue/asthenia (26.6%), ALT or AST increased (14.4% each), nausea (13.5%), and anemia (12.2%). <sentence_start/>The most common AE grade ≥ 3 were neutropenia, hypokalemia (1.9% each), anemia, QT prolongation, and hypertension (1.6% each, Table 1) [<citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2505725" pmid="40454645" count="1">52</citation>].

Lasofoxifene is a next-generation SERM and has been tested against fulvestrant in the phase II ELAINE-1 trial in an exclusively <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated cohort progressing on AI and CDK4/6i therapy. <sentence_start/>The trial was negative for its primary endpoint, PFS [median 5.6 months for lasofoxifene and 3.4 months for fulvestrant; HR 0.70 (95% CI 0.43-1.15); <italic>P</italic> = 0.14] [<citation rid="B53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2023.09.3104" pmid="38072514" count="1">53</citation>].

CERANs are another novel class of drugs targeting the ER and function as complete estrogen antagonists by blocking the ligand-binding pocket of the ER. <sentence_start/>Palazestrant is currently being evaluated in the phase III OPERA-01 trial in endocrine-resistant, CDK4/6i pretreated patients against endocrine monotherapy [<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2023.102569" pmid="37146385" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="B54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/14796694.2025.2608863" pmid="41461598" pmcid="PMC12802986" count="1">54</citation>].

In conclusion, the three endocrine agents elacestrant, imlunestrant, and vepdegestrant have each demonstrated efficacy as monotherapy in randomized phase III trials; with an <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated subgroup included as the primary analysis population. <sentence_start/>While elacestrant showed a PFS benefit across a biomarker-unselected and the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated population, the benefit with imlunestrant and vepdegestrant was confined to the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated subgroup [<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.00338" pmid="35584336" pmcid="PMC9553388" count="1">41</citation>, <citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2505725" pmid="40454645" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings should be interpreted in the context of some methodological considerations regarding trial design and cross-trial heterogeneity complicating treatment comparisons (Table 2). <sentence_start/>All three trials employed ET monotherapy as control treatment, which may not reflect current clinical practice where combination approaches are increasingly preferred. <sentence_start/>Comparator selection differed across trials, which is a relevant aspect as suboptimal treatment in the control arm may inflate observed treatment effects. <sentence_start/>While prior fulvestrant was an exclusion criterion in both the vepdegestrant and imlunestrant trials-consistent with fulvestrant being the control treatment-a minority of patients in the imlunestrant trials received AI therapy as control treatment despite mandatory AI preexposure; and in the elacestrant trial, both fulvestrant and AI were used as control treatments despite prior exposure being allowed. <sentence_start/>In addition, CDK4/6i pretreatment was mandatory only in the vepdegestrant and elacestrant trials, limiting applicability of the imlunestrant results to a post-CDK4/6i setting [<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.00338" pmid="35584336" pmcid="PMC9553388" count="1">41</citation>, <citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2505725" pmid="40454645" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Moreover, the included population was heavily pretreated in the elacestrant trial, which may have attenuated the observed treatment effect, as treatment efficacy generally decreases with increasing lines of systemic therapy [<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.00338" pmid="35584336" pmcid="PMC9553388" count="1">41</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Across the three trials, patients with indeterminate <italic>ESR1</italic> mutational status were classified and analyzed as <italic>ESR1</italic>-non-detectable. <sentence_start/>However, reporting of the prevalence of <italic>ESR1</italic>-negative and <italic>ESR1-</italic>indeterminate within the <italic>ESR1</italic>-non-detectable group was inconsistent between trials, and <italic>ESR1</italic> mutational status was not a stratification factor in all three trials (Table 3) [<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.00338" pmid="35584336" pmcid="PMC9553388" count="1">41</citation>, <citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2505725" pmid="40454645" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Camizestrant as monotherapy only demonstrated activity in a phase II setting, with the clinically relevant subgroup of patients with CDK4/6i preexposure limited to fewer than 40 patients per arm; the clinical significance of these findings therefore remains to be confirmed in a larger trial [<citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(24)00387-5" pmid="39481395" count="1">44</citation>].
CDK4/6i post CDK4/6i-progression: identical CDK4/6i, switch of ET

Given the modest efficacy of endocrine monotherapy following progression on ET and CDK4/6i, the selection of a combination therapy may be favored as a further line therapy. <sentence_start/>A biomarker-independent strategy consists of either switching to a different endocrine agent and a different CDK4/6i, or switching to an alternative ET while maintaining the same CDK4/6i beyond progression on both agents.

The phase II PALMIRA trial evaluated the continuation of palbociclib beyond disease progression by randomizing patients previously treated with palbociclib plus an AI or fulvestrant to receive either ET alone or ET with continued palbociclib. <sentence_start/>The trial did not meet the primary endpoint of PFS [<citation rid="B55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco-24-01865" pmid="40294349" pmcid="PMC12169856" count="1">55</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, the phase II PACE trial randomized patients progressing on an AI plus CDK4/6i therapy (palbociclib in 91% of patients) to fulvestrant alone or fulvestrant plus palbociclib, but did not demonstrate a PFS benefit for the combination therapy [<citation rid="B56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.23.01940" pmid="38513188" count="1">56</citation>].

Two extensively debated trials introduced a novel treatment approach, in which therapy was not switched upon clinically evident progression, but upon emergence of a molecular marker of progression [<citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2502929" pmid="40454637" count="1">45</citation>, <citation rid="B57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1470-2045(22)00555-1" pmid="36183733" count="1">57</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similar to PALMIRA and PACE, the PADA-1 trial evaluated an ET switch with continued CDK4/6 inhibition. <sentence_start/>Notably, the treatment was changed at the time of molecular progression-defined by rising <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-rather than at clinical progression on first-line AI and palbociclib. <sentence_start/>Patients with rising <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations were randomized to continue AI plus palbociclib or switch to fulvestrant plus palbociclib. <sentence_start/>This strategy was associated with a significant improvement in the primary endpoint PFS in favor of the molecularly triggered treatment switch [updated analysis: median PFS 12.8 months and 5.9 months for switch to fulvestrant and continuation of AI, respectively; HR 0.54 (95% CI 0.38-0.75); <italic>P</italic> = 0.0003] [<citation rid="B57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1470-2045(22)00555-1" pmid="36183733" count="1">57</citation>, <citation rid="B58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.002" pmid="41260263" count="1">58</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Sixty-eight percent of patients in the control arm crossed over to fulvestrant plus palbociclib after clinically evident progression, with a median PFS of 3.5 months in this subsequent line. <sentence_start/>The secondary endpoint median time to strategy failure, i.e., time from randomization to time of palbociclib and ET discontinuation or death, was 11.9 months for the switch-fulvestrant-group and 10.6 months for the AI-continuation group [HR 1.02 (95% CI 0.71-1.45); <italic>P</italic> = 0.9; from primary analysis]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, the median chemotherapy-free survival was 14.6 months in the fulvestrant-switch group compared with 13.1 months in the AI-continuation group [HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.62-1.33); secondary endpoint, <italic>P</italic> = 0.6, from primary analysis] [<citation rid="B57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1470-2045(22)00555-1" pmid="36183733" count="1">57</citation>]. <sentence_start/>OS data were still immature [<citation rid="B58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.002" pmid="41260263" count="1">58</citation>].

Analogous to PADA-1, SERENA-6 investigated a treatment switch triggered by the detection of <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations by ctDNA prior to clinically evident progression<italic>.</italic> <sentence_start/>Patients on first-line AI plus CDK4/6i therapy (palbociclib in 76% of patients) were randomized upon <italic>ESR1</italic> mutation detection to either continue the same regimen or to switch the endocrine backbone to the oral SERD camizestrant, while maintaining the same CDK4/6i. <sentence_start/>Crossover to an oral SERD with CDK4/6i continuation was not allowed in the control arm. <sentence_start/>In patients with a detectable <italic>ESR1</italic> mutation who were randomized to the respective treatments, PFS was significantly prolonged with camizestrant and CDK4/6i in comparison to continuation of the initial regimen [median PFS 16 months vs. 9.2 months; HR 0.44 (95% CI 0.31-0.60); <italic>P</italic> < 0.0001]. <sentence_start/>Results for PFS2, which in principle compares an unequal number of sequentially administered therapeutic substances between groups, were immature at first analysis [HR 0.52 (95% CI 0.33-0.81); <italic>P</italic> = 0.004, prespecified significance threshold <italic>P</italic> = 0.0001]. <sentence_start/>OS data were immature [<citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2502929" pmid="40454637" count="1">45</citation>].

The PADA-1 and SERENA-6 trials were notable for the pioneering approach to guide treatment decisions based on detection of molecularly defined progression. <sentence_start/>Beyond the aspiration to improve survival outcomes, potential advantages of a molecularly guided switching approach may theoretically include the prevention of tumor-progression-related complications, symptoms and clinical deterioration, and possible reduction of clinical and financial toxicity from an increasingly ineffective treatment. <sentence_start/>Despite both trials being positive for their primary endpoint, PFS, this endpoint design does not allow for a conclusion whether switching upon molecular instead of clinical progression is superior in efficacy, given the inherent imbalance of active substances between treatment arms. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the lack of differences in median time to strategy failure and chemotherapy-free survival between the two arms in PADA-1 does not appear to indicate a benefit of therapy adaptation upon molecular rather than clinically evident progression. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, the definition of molecular progression represents a conceptual challenge. <sentence_start/>Longitudinal ctDNA analyses from PADA-1 suggest that <italic>ESR1</italic> mutation detectability is dynamic, with fluctuations and occasional loss of detection occurring independently of treatment changes, including in the AI plus CDK4/6i arm [<citation rid="B58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.002" pmid="41260263" count="1">58</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This might challenge the classification of <italic>ESR1</italic> positivity, its direct attribution as a biomarker of relevant molecular progression, and underscores the need for standardized assays and uniform definitions to reduce risk of possible overtreatment. <sentence_start/>In addition, the feasibility of regular ctDNA monitoring needs to be determined across all healthcare settings, and associated surveillance demands might carry implications for patient experience and health systems.

In summary, switching the endocrine backbone to fulvestrant while maintaining the same CDK4/6i upon clinical progression has only been investigated for palbociclib and did not improve efficacy [<citation rid="B55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco-24-01865" pmid="40294349" pmcid="PMC12169856" count="1">55</citation>, <citation rid="B56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.23.01940" pmid="38513188" count="1">56</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Molecularly guided switching strategies of the endocrine agent on first-line AI and CDK4/6i represent a novel approach with potentially beneficial implications, yet convincing evidence of superiority in efficacy is currently lacking, and questions regarding practical implementation and implications for patients and health system resources remain open [<citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2502929" pmid="40454637" count="1">45</citation>, <citation rid="B57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1470-2045(22)00555-1" pmid="36183733" count="1">57</citation>, <citation rid="B58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.002" pmid="41260263" count="1">58</citation>].
CDK4/6i post CDK4/6i-progression: switch of CDK4/6i and switch of ET

In the phase II MAINTAIN trial, patients progressing on ET and CDK4/6i (palbociclib in 87% of patients) in the advanced setting underwent a switch to an alternative ET (fulvestrant or AI), either as monotherapy or in combination with ribociclib. <sentence_start/>Switching ET plus ribociclib led to improved PFS compared to switching to an alternative ET monotherapy [median PFS 5.3 vs. 2.8 months; HR 0.57 (95% CI 0.39-0.85); <italic>P</italic> = 0.006]. <sentence_start/>No OS analysis was reported [<citation rid="B59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.02392" pmid="37207300" count="1">59</citation>].

Similarly, in the phase III postMONARCH trial, patients progressing on AI plus CDK4/6i therapy were switched to fulvestrant monotherapy or fulvestrant in combination with abemaciclib. <sentence_start/>Palbociclib was the most common prior CDK4/6i (59% of patients), followed by ribociclib (33%) and abemaciclib (8%). <sentence_start/>The addition of abemaciclib led to a statistically significant PFS benefit [median PFS 6.0 vs. 5.3 months, and 6-month PFS rates 50% vs. 37% for the combination therapy and fulvestrant, respectively; HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.57-0.95); <italic>P</italic> = 0.017]. <sentence_start/>Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested a potential benefit among patients with prior palbociclib exposure [HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.44-0.86)], while no effect was observed in the small subgroup of ribociclib-pretreated patients [HR 1.01 (95% CI 0.67-1.51)]. <sentence_start/>However, the interaction <italic>p</italic>-value was not significant. <sentence_start/>OS data were immature [<citation rid="B60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco-24-02086" pmid="39693591" pmcid="PMC11936477" count="1">60</citation>].

The approach of simultaneous endocrine and CDK4/6i switch has been modified to the use of oral SERDs instead of fulvestrant for potentially better efficacy and a more convenient oral formulation. <sentence_start/>In the three-arm phase III EMBER-3 trial, imlunestrant plus abemaciclib was superior to imlunestrant monotherapy after progression on an AI, which had been combined with a CDK4/6i in 65% of patients (palbociclib in 63%, ribociclib in 27%, and abemaciclib in 8% of cases) [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The combination of imlunestrant and abemaciclib was superior to imlunestrant alone with respect to the primary endpoint PFS in the ITT population [median PFS 10.9 vs. 5.5 months; HR 0.59 (95% CI 0.47-0.74); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001] [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A benefit for the combination therapy was observed in a prespecified exploratory analysis both among patients with prior CDK4/6i treatment [median PFS 9.1 vs. 3.7 months; HR 0.53 (95% CI 0.40-0.69)] and across <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated and non-mutated subgroups [<citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>OS data were not mature yet [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>].

In the single-arm phase II ELAINE-2 trial, which exclusively enrolled patients with <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated disease, lasofoxifene plus abemaciclib demonstrated encouraging activity (median PFS 13 months and overall response rate (ORR) 56%) in a more heavily pretreated population allowing previous ET, chemotherapy, and multiple CDK4/6i exposures [<citation rid="B61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2023.09.3103" pmid="38072513" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This combination will be compared against abemaciclib and fulvestrant in the phase III ELAINE-3 trial in <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated disease following progression on CDK4/6i and AI, addressing the need for head-to-head comparisons of combination therapies [<citation rid="B62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/14796694.2025.2481825" pmid="40222048" pmcid="PMC12051526" count="1">62</citation>].

Taken together, after progression on ET plus CDK4/6i, switching ET and adding abemaciclib or ribociclib improved PFS vs. endocrine monotherapy [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>, <citation rid="B59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.02392" pmid="37207300" count="1">59</citation>, <citation rid="B60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco-24-02086" pmid="39693591" pmcid="PMC11936477" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, this benefit has mainly been shown after prior palbociclib, and its efficacy following abemaciclib or ribociclib remains less certain [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>, <citation rid="B59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.02392" pmid="37207300" count="1">59</citation>, <citation rid="B60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco-24-02086" pmid="39693591" pmcid="PMC11936477" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The approach of combining imlunestrant with abemaciclib demonstrated a median PFS of 10.9 months, which appears to be an encouraging result. <sentence_start/>However, the notable limitation of only 61% CDK4/6i pretreatment complicates comparison with other regimens and limits applicability to the post-CDK4/6i setting [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>].
Therapeutic combinations targeting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway

The PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway plays an important role in cell proliferation, growth, survival, and metabolism [<citation rid="B63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2024.102861" pmid="39662202" count="1">63</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Intracellular activation of the lipid kinase PI3K leads to recruitment of the serine/threonine kinase AKT, which is further activated through phosphorylation by mTORC2. mTORC1 and 2 represent two complexes with distinct functions that both incorporate the serine/threonine kinase mTOR. <sentence_start/>Activated AKT is a central signaling node of the pathway and mediates further downstream signaling on multiple target proteins, including activation of mTORC1 among downstream consequences. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the phosphatase PTEN inhibits PI3K/AKT signaling by antagonizing AKT activation [<citation rid="B63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2024.102861" pmid="39662202" count="1">63</citation>, <citation rid="B64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(23)00676-9" pmid="38547898" count="1">64</citation>].

In HR+/HER2- ABC, the mTOR inhibitor everolimus was the first clinically introduced substance to interfere with the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and inhibits mTORC1 [<citation rid="B64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(23)00676-9" pmid="38547898" count="1">64</citation>, <citation rid="B65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2017.07.005" pmid="28779636" count="1">65</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Everolimus showed therapeutic efficacy in clinical trials in an endocrine-resistant population in combination with ET in the pre-CDK4/6i-era [<citation rid="B66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2017.76.9331" pmid="29664714" pmcid="PMC7186582" count="1">66</citation>-<citation rid="B68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1109653" pmid="22149876" pmcid="PMC5705195" count="1">68</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Treatment with everolimus has not been biomarker-guided, and an association with treatment efficacy with <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutation has not been established [<citation rid="B69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2014.60.1971" pmid="26503204" pmcid="PMC5070556" count="1">69</citation>, <citation rid="B70" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/bjc.2017.25" pmid="28183140" pmcid="PMC5355930" count="1">70</citation>].

More recently, approaches targeting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway in combination with fulvestrant in a biomarker-selected population have been implemented in the treatment landscape of HR+/HER2- ABC: In contrast to <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations acquired during treatment, <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations-encoding the catalytic subunit of PI3K (p110α)-are mostly considered early, tumor-intrinsic (“truncal”) events and have been observed in up to approximately 35-45% of HR+/HER2- breast cancers, although there is evidence demonstrating spatial and temporal heterogeneity [<citation rid="B71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.cd-20-1647" pmid="34183353" pmcid="PMC9414283" count="1">71</citation>-<citation rid="B75" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10549-023-07010-1" pmid="37392328" pmcid="PMC10361863" count="1">75</citation>].

The PI3K inhibitor alpelisib was the first PI3K inhibitor implemented in the treatment of HR+/HER2- ABC [<citation rid="B76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1813904" pmid="31091374" count="1">76</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Alpelisib targets the p110α subunit of PI3K [<citation rid="B64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(23)00676-9" pmid="38547898" count="1">64</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In endocrine-pretreated patients, alpelisib plus fulvestrant demonstrated superiority over fulvestrant for the primary endpoint PFS in a <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated population [median PFS 11 vs. 5.7 months for the combination therapy vs. fulvestrant, respectively; HR 0.65 (95% CI 0.50-0.85); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001] in the phase III SOLAR-1 trial. <sentence_start/>For the secondary endpoint of PFS in the <italic>PIK3CA</italic> wild-type (WT) patients, no significant effect could be demonstrated [<citation rid="B76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1813904" pmid="31091374" count="1">76</citation>]. <sentence_start/>No significant OS benefit was observed [<citation rid="B77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2020.11.011" pmid="33246021" count="1">77</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Given that only 6% of patients had received prior CDK4/6i therapy, this treatment was further evaluated in the single-arm BYLieve trial requiring prior CDK4/6i exposure, confirming efficacy in this population (median PFS 8.0 months) [<citation rid="B76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1813904" pmid="31091374" count="1">76</citation>, <citation rid="B78" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(24)00673-9" pmid="39637900" count="1">78</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, alpelisib was associated with relevant toxicity, with a treatment discontinuation rate due to AEs of 26%. <sentence_start/>The most common grade 3-4 AEs were hyperglycemia (37%), rash (10%), and diarrhea (7%) [<citation rid="B77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2020.11.011" pmid="33246021" count="1">77</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Results of the phase III EPIK-B5 trial, available in abstract form only, provided evidence of a significant PFS benefit (primary endpoint) of alpelisib when added to fulvestrant in a post-CDK4/6i and AI setting in an exclusively <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated population [median PFS 7.4 vs. 2.8 months; HR 0.52 (95% CI 0.37-0.72); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001]. <sentence_start/>The authors stated a positive trend for OS, with a median OS of 29.5 vs. 23.8 months in the control arm [HR 0.64 (95% CI 0.41-0.99); <italic>P</italic> = 0.021]. <sentence_start/>Statistical significance was not explicitly claimed, and formal interpretation of this <italic>P</italic>-value awaits full publication [<citation rid="B79" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1557-3265.sabcs25-rf7-02" count="1">79</citation>].

Inavolisib, a selective p110α inhibitor that also degrades mutant p110α, has been incorporated into first-line therapy for HR+/HER2- breast cancer in combination with palbociclib and fulvestrant in patients with a <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutation [<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2501796" pmid="40454641" pmcid="PMC13496148" count="1">26</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Inavolisib plus fulvestrant is being evaluated vs. alpelisib plus fulvestrant in patients with <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated disease after CDK4/6i therapy in the phase III INAVO121 trial, thereby generating important clinical evidence for direct comparisons between endocrine combination therapies [<citation rid="B80" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2024.42.16_suppl.tps1136" count="1">80</citation>].

The novel, allosteric PI3Kα inhibitor zovegalisib is designed to target mutant PI3Kα while sparing the WT variant, with the aim of reducing the side effects of PI3Kα-inhibitors [<citation rid="B64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(23)00676-9" pmid="38547898" count="1">64</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the phase III ReDiscover-2 trial, zovegalisib plus fulvestrant is being tested against capivasertib and fulvestrant in a CDK4/6i pretreated population with <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutation, providing important direct comparisons of combination therapies [<citation rid="B81" ref-type="bibr" count="1">81</citation>].

Apart from mutations in <italic>PIK3CA,</italic> the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway can be activated by less prevalent mutations in <italic>AKT1</italic> (5-7% in ABC) and by loss of PTEN function (5-10% of breast cancers), both resulting in AKT activation [<citation rid="B64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(23)00676-9" pmid="38547898" count="1">64</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The selective AKT inhibitor capivasertib targets PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activation driven by genomic alterations in <italic>PIK3CA</italic>, <italic>AKT1</italic>, or <italic>PTEN.</italic> <sentence_start/>In combination with fulvestrant, capivasertib demonstrated superiority over fulvestrant in the randomized phase III CAPItello-291 trial. <sentence_start/>Eligible patients had endocrine-resistant advanced HR+/HER2- breast cancer; 70% had prior exposure to CDK4/6i and 18% had received chemotherapy for advanced disease. <sentence_start/>Forty-one percent of patients had a confirmed PI3K-AKT pathway alteration, with activating <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations in 31%, activating <italic>AKT1</italic> mutations in 5%, and inactivating <italic>PTEN</italic> alterations in 5% of patients. <sentence_start/>Of note, PI3K-AKT pathway alteration status was not assessed before inclusion and not used as a stratification factor at randomization; 15% of patients enrolled had an unknown alteration status (Table 3). <sentence_start/>Capivasertib plus fulvestrant significantly improved PFS for both primary endpoints: in the ITT population [median PFS 7.2 vs. 3.6 months; HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.51-0.71); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001] and in patients with a PI3K-AKT pathway alteration [median PFS 7.3 vs. 3.1 months; HR 0.50 (95% CI 0.38-0.65); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001]. <sentence_start/>Exploratory subgroup analysis suggested a benefit irrespective of CDK4/6i pretreatment in the ITT population. <sentence_start/>An exploratory analysis in the PI3K-AKT pathway-non-altered population, performed after exclusion of the 25% of patients with unknown molecular status, suggested no clear PFS benefit in this subgroup [HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.61-1.02)]. <sentence_start/>The most common grade ≥ 3 AEs were rash (12%), followed by diarrhea (9%) and hyperglycemia (2.3%). <sentence_start/>Treatment discontinuation due to AEs occurred in 13% of patients [<citation rid="B82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2214131" pmid="37256976" pmcid="PMC11335038" count="1">82</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Capivasertib in combination with fulvestrant and a CDK4/6i is investigated against fulvestrant and CDK4/6i in patients experiencing endocrine-resistant disease in the adjuvant setting in the phase III CAPItello-292 trial [<citation rid="B83" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1538-7445.sabcs23-po2-19-10" count="1">83</citation>].

Evidence on another AKT inhibitor, ipatasertib, is currently available as an abstract only, and demonstrated a significant PFS benefit in combination with fulvestrant vs. fulvestrant alone in the phase III CCTG/BCT MA.40/FINER trial. <sentence_start/>Eligible patients had advanced HR+/HER2- breast cancer progressing on AI and CDK4/6i. <sentence_start/>The trial was positive for PFS in the ITT population [primary analysis, median PFS 5.3 vs. 1.9 months; HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.46-0.81); <italic>P</italic> = 0.0007], as well as in the PI3K-AKT pathway-altered cohort (secondary analysis), i.e., with genomic alterations in <italic>PIK3CA</italic>, <italic>AKT1,</italic> or <italic>PTEN</italic> [median PFS 5.5 vs. 1.9 months; HR 0.47 (95% CI 0.31-0.72); <italic>P</italic> = 0.0005]. <sentence_start/>The most common non-hematological grade ≥ 3 AEs were diarrhea (16%), fatigue (3%), vomiting, and rash (2% each). <sentence_start/>Treatment discontinuation rate due to AEs was 6.5% [<citation rid="B84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2025.43.17_suppl.lba1005" count="1">84</citation>].

In contrast to the previously discussed trials evaluating PI3K and AKT inhibitors with fulvestrant as ET backbone [<citation rid="B79" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1557-3265.sabcs25-rf7-02" count="1">79</citation>, <citation rid="B82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2214131" pmid="37256976" pmcid="PMC11335038" count="1">82</citation>, <citation rid="B84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2025.43.17_suppl.lba1005" count="1">84</citation>], the mTOR inhibitor everolimus has been investigated in combination with the oral SERD giredestrant in the phase III evERA trial [<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.09.026" count="1">50</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Patients were included upon progression following ET and CDK4/6i and were randomized to either giredestrant plus everolimus or IC ET (i.e., exemestane, fulvestrant or tamoxifen) plus everolimus. <sentence_start/>The trial was positive for both primary endpoints PFS in the ITT [median PFS 8.8 vs. 5.5 months; HR 0.56 (95% CI 0.44-0.71); <italic>P</italic> < 0.0001] and in the <italic>ESR1-</italic>mutated cohort [median PFS 10 vs. 5.5 months; HR 0.38 (95% CI 0.27-0.54); <italic>P</italic> < 0.0001, presented as abstract] [<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.09.026" count="1">50</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Full trial publication, along with its clinical positioning within the treatment landscape, remains pending. <sentence_start/>A clear strength of the trial was the incorporation of a combination-therapy regimen as comparator treatment [<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.09.026" count="1">50</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Everolimus in combination with the oral SERD elacestrant vs. elacestrant monotherapy is currently investigated in the randomized phase III ADELA trial in the post-CDK4/6i setting in an exclusively <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated population [<citation rid="B85" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2025.43.16_suppl.tps1129" count="1">85</citation>].

Similar to the triplet combination strategy of ET, CDK4/6i and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway targeting evaluated in the first-line INAVO120 trial [<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2501796" pmid="40454641" pmcid="PMC13496148" count="1">26</citation>], the phase III VIKTORIA-1 trial investigated gedatolisib, palbociclib, and fulvestrant in CDK4/6i pretreated patients [<citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Gedatolisib is a multitarget inhibitor targeting both PI3K and mTORC1/2. <sentence_start/>The two-part, three-arm trial investigated both <italic>i)</italic> the triplet combination gedatolisib, palbociclib, and fulvestrant and the doublet <italic>ii)</italic> gedatolisib and fulvestrant vs. <italic>iii)</italic> fulvestrant monotherapy. <sentence_start/>No prior exposure to chemotherapy or ADCs in the advanced setting was allowed. <sentence_start/>Fulvestrant pretreatment was allowed, but the number of fulvestrant-pretreated patients was not reported. <sentence_start/>Forty percent of patients had prior palbociclib exposure; 49% ribociclib and 17% prior abemaciclib. <sentence_start/>Parts 1 and 2 of the study enrolled patients with <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-WT and <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated tumors, respectively. <sentence_start/>In part 1, PFS was significantly prolonged with the triplet therapy compared to fulvestrant [median PFS 9.3 vs. 2.0 months; HR 0.24 (95% CI 0.17-0.35); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001] and with the doublet therapy compared to fulvestrant [median PFS 7.4 vs. 2.0 months; HR 0.33 (95% CI 0.24-0.48); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001]. <sentence_start/>The most common grade ≥ 3 treatment-related AEs were neutropenia (62.3% and 0.8% in the triplet and doublet combination group, respectively), stomatitis (19.2% and 12.3%), leukopenia (6.2% and 0%), rash (4.6% and 5.4%), nausea (3.8% and 0.8%), hyperglycemia (2.3% for both groups) and diarrhea (1.5% and 0.8%). <sentence_start/>Treatment-related AEs led to treatment discontinuation in 2.3% of patients in the triplet combination group and 3.1% in the doublet combination group. <sentence_start/>Two treatment-related deaths occurred with the triplet combination (pneumonia and hepatic failure) [<citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>].

In conclusion, alpelisib represents a treatment option in the endocrine-resistant management of <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated HR+/HER2- ABC, supported by a PFS benefit, but in the absence of an OS benefit [<citation rid="B76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1813904" pmid="31091374" count="1">76</citation>, <citation rid="B77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2020.11.011" pmid="33246021" count="1">77</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Fully published trial evidence in the post-CDK4/6i setting still derives, at present, from single-arm phase II data [<citation rid="B78" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(24)00673-9" pmid="39637900" count="1">78</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Capivasertib has been incorporated in the same therapeutic setting for tumors harboring a PI3K-AKT pathway alteration, after demonstration of a PFS benefit in an only partially CDK4/6i pretreated population [<citation rid="B82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2214131" pmid="37256976" pmcid="PMC11335038" count="1">82</citation>]. <sentence_start/>While alpelisib and capivasertib exhibit a partially overlapping, class-related toxicity profile, the safety profile reported for capivasertib is considered more favorable, particularly with regard to severe hyperglycemia [<citation rid="B77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2020.11.011" pmid="33246021" count="1">77</citation>, <citation rid="B82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2214131" pmid="37256976" pmcid="PMC11335038" count="1">82</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It should be clearly emphasized, however, that this observation is based on cross-trial comparison. <sentence_start/>With PFS benefits shown for both its dual and triplet combinations, gedatolisib emerges as a potential treatment option in the absence of <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutation [<citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In patients with <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-WT disease, it would have its position as an alternative to previously biomarker-unselected strategies. <sentence_start/>Though promising, to date, gedatolisib has not yet received Food and Drug Administration (FDA) nor European Medicines Agency (EMA) approval [<citation rid="B87" ref-type="bibr" count="1">87</citation>, <citation rid="B88" ref-type="bibr" count="1">88</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Across the three trials, fulvestrant served as the control arm, not reflecting the current SOC in most cases. <sentence_start/>The trials further differed in their pretreatment inclusion criteria-especially relevant with respect to prior fulvestrant and CDK4/6i exposure-and biomarker stratification (Tables 2 and 3); possibly affecting observed treatment effects [<citation rid="B76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1813904" pmid="31091374" count="1">76</citation>, <citation rid="B82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2214131" pmid="37256976" pmcid="PMC11335038" count="1">82</citation>, <citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The clinical positioning of the ipatasertib-fulvestrant and everolimus-giredestrant combinations within the treatment landscape awaits the full publication of the respective trials [<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.09.026" count="1">50</citation>, <citation rid="B84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2025.43.17_suppl.lba1005" count="1">84</citation>].

Poly(ADP-ribose)-polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) represent a non-endocrine-based alternative for patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline <italic>BRCA1/2</italic> (<italic>gBRCA1/2</italic>) and somatic <italic>BRCA1/2</italic> (<italic>sBRCA1/2</italic>) mutations, and mutations in germline <italic>PALB2</italic> (<italic>gPALB2</italic>) [<citation rid="B89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/annonc/mdz012" pmid="30689707" pmcid="PMC6503629" count="1">89</citation>-<citation rid="B92" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02075" pmid="41604601" count="1">92</citation>].

Two phase III trials tested the PARPi olaparib (OlympiAD) and talazoparib (EMBRACA) against chemotherapy in HER2- ABC in patients with <italic>gBRCA1/2</italic>-mutations with a maximum of three previous chemotherapy regimens and no limit on previous hormonal therapies (EMBRACA) or a maximum of two previous chemotherapies and at least one previous hormonal therapy (OlympiAD). <sentence_start/>Importantly, these studies were performed before the introduction of CDK4/6i. <sentence_start/>Both trials reported a significant PFS benefit in the ITT population [olaparib: median PFS 7.0 vs. 4.2 months, HR 0.58 (95% CI 0.43-0.80); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001; talazoparib: median PFS 8.6 vs. 5.6 months, HR 0.54 (95% CI 0.41-0.71); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001], but no improvement in OS was observed [<citation rid="B89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/annonc/mdz012" pmid="30689707" pmcid="PMC6503629" count="1">89</citation>, <citation rid="B91" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2020.08.2098" pmid="32828825" pmcid="PMC10649377" count="1">91</citation>, <citation rid="B93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1802905" pmid="30110579" pmcid="PMC10600918" count="1">93</citation>, <citation rid="B94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa1706450" pmid="28578601" count="1">94</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Exploratory subgroup analyses of the respective trials suggested a PFS benefit for olaparib in the triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) population, but not in HR+/HER2- disease, whereas talazoparib led to improvement in median PFS regardless of subtype [<citation rid="B93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1802905" pmid="30110579" pmcid="PMC10600918" count="1">93</citation>, <citation rid="B94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa1706450" pmid="28578601" count="1">94</citation>].

To contextualize the role of PARPi in a treatment landscape after CDK4/6i exposure, a retrospective multi-site analysis suggested a real-world PFS of 8.5 months for talazoparib in HR+/HER2- patients who were mainly pretreated with CDK4/6i [<citation rid="B95" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyad021" pmid="36952230" pmcid="PMC10166159" count="1">95</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the phase IIIb LUCY study, no signal of reduced olaparib efficacy was observed in patients with prior CDK4/6i exposure (<italic>n</italic> = 25, median PFS 9.1 months) compared with CDK4/6i-naïve patients (<italic>n</italic> = 12, median PFS 8.4 months), although subgroup sizes were unequal and not formally compared [<citation rid="B96" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10549-023-07165-x" pmid="38112922" pmcid="PMC10948524" count="1">96</citation>].

The phase II TBCRC 048 trial provided a signal of anti-tumor efficacy regarding ORR (primary endpoint) of olaparib in patients with mutations in <italic>gPALB2</italic> (ORR 68% in HR+/HER2- disease, <italic>n</italic> = 19) or with tumors that contain a mutation in s<italic>BRCA1/2</italic> (ORR of 36% in HR+/HER2- disease, <italic>n</italic> = 33). <sentence_start/>The vast majority of HR+/HER2- patients were CDK4/6i pretreated [<citation rid="B92" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02075" pmid="41604601" count="1">92</citation>]. <sentence_start/>No relevant activity was observed for <italic>ATM</italic> or <italic>CHEK2</italic> mutations [<citation rid="B90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.20.02151" pmid="33119476" count="1">90</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Based on these data, testing for <italic>gBRCA1/2</italic> is recommended to guide treatment strategy in HR+/HER2- breast cancer, as is testing for <italic>gPALB2</italic> and <italic>sBRCA1/2,</italic> although with a lower level of evidence and weaker recommendation [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>].

Chemotherapies, including ADCs, become relevant once endocrine (combination) therapies are exhausted or a rapid tumor response is clinically indicated. <sentence_start/>Single-agent chemotherapy has been preferred over combination chemotherapy in this setting due to the lack of an OS benefit with combination regimens, except if a rapid response is needed. <sentence_start/>Generally, taxanes and anthracyclines are the preferred agents, unless there was a recent exposure [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Other treatment options include capecitabine, eribulin, vinorelbine, gemcitabine, or platinum agents [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Adding bevacizumab to capecitabine or a taxane is an option, having demonstrated a PFS benefit in the absence of an OS benefit [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>].

The role of chemotherapy as “first non-endocrine based therapy” has been challenged by the results of the DESTINY-Breast06 trial investigating the anti-HER2 ADC trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) in
