HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer patients with progression on endocrine-based therapy, including CDK4/6i, but no prior use of chemotherapy for advanced disease. <sentence_start/>Additionally, tumors were required to demonstrate HER2-low staining assessed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) (IHC score 1+ or 2+ and negative in situ hybridization/ISH) or HER2-ultralow expression (IHC 0 with membrane staining; IHC > 0 and < 1+). <sentence_start/>Eighty-two percent of patients had HER2-low disease, 89% had prior CDK4/6i exposure, and 41% and 47% had prior anthracycline and taxane therapy, respectively, in the curative setting. <sentence_start/>T-DXd significantly improved PFS vs. physician’s choice of chemotherapy (capecitabine, nab-paclitaxel, or paclitaxel) in the HER2-low population [primary endpoint, median PFS 13.2 vs. 8.1 months; HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.52-0.75); <italic>P</italic> < 0.001]. <sentence_start/>ORR was 57% for T-DXd and 32% for chemotherapy in the HER2-low population. <sentence_start/>The prespecified exploratory analysis of patients with HER2-ultralow disease (18% of patients) showed a numerical trend in PFS in favor of T-DXd [median PFS 13.2 months for T-DXd and 8.3 months for chemotherapy; HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.50-1.21)]. <sentence_start/>Exploratory analysis of ORR in the HER2-ultralow population was 62% with T-DXd (vs. 26% with chemotherapy) [<citation rid="B97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa2407086" pmid="39282896" count="1">97</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The three most commonly observed drug-related AEs of any severity with T-DXd were nausea, fatigue, and alopecia; and the most common grade ≥ 3 events were neutropenia (20.7%), anemia (5.8%), and fatigue (3.7%). <sentence_start/>Drug-related interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pneumonitis occurred in 11.3% of patients (grade ≥ 3 in 1.4%, and grade 5 events in 0.7%); and left ventricular dysfunction/ejection fraction decrease was observed in 8.1% of patients (grade ≥ 3 in 0.7%, no grade 5 events and no reporting of cardiac failure) [<citation rid="B97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa2407086" pmid="39282896" count="1">97</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Given the pending OS data from this trial, and considering the OS benefit observed in HER2-low disease in DESTINY-Breast04-which evaluated T-DXd after one prior line of chemotherapy-clinicians may currently decide on a case-by-case basis between T-DXd and chemotherapy after CDK4/6i therapy and potentially other endocrine-based therapy lines [<citation rid="B98" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2203690" pmid="35665782" pmcid="PMC10561652" count="1">98</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In DESTINY-Breast04 and 06, patients with brain metastases were included, but comprised a minority of patients (5-8% of the HR+ population) [<citation rid="B97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa2407086" pmid="39282896" count="1">97</citation>, <citation rid="B98" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2203690" pmid="35665782" pmcid="PMC10561652" count="1">98</citation>]. <sentence_start/>An exploratory subgroup analysis of patients with brain metastases (<italic>n</italic> = 24, 75% HR+/HER2- tumors) from the DESTINY-Breast04 trial (presented as an abstract), showed an intracranial ORR of 25% with T-DXd, but no intracranial response in patients treated with single-agent chemotherapy (<italic>n</italic> = 11) [<citation rid="B99" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2023.09.565" count="1">99</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A single-arm phase II trial with 12 patients with more heavily pretreated, HER2-low disease (75% HR+) showed an ORR of 50% in asymptomatic untreated and 33% in patients with progressing brain metastases [<citation rid="B100" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.esmoop.2024.103699" pmid="39255534" pmcid="PMC11415677" count="1">100</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Overall, these results indicate that T-DXd demonstrates significant intracranial activity in patients with HR+/HER2-low ABC and brain metastases. <sentence_start/>Another HER2-directed ADC, BNT323/DB-1303, is under investigation against single-agent chemotherapy in HR+/HER2-low ABC after prior ET and possibly CDK4/6i treatment, but no chemotherapy exposure for advanced disease [<citation rid="B101" ref-type="bibr" count="1">101</citation>].

In contrast, based on data available in abstract form only, the TROP2-directed ADC sacituzumab govitecan (SG) did not demonstrate a benefit vs. single-agent chemotherapy when being evaluated in the phase III ASCENT-07 trial in patients with HR+/HER2- ABC after progression on ET and mostly prior CDK4/6i therapy, but no previous chemotherapy for advanced disease [<citation rid="B102" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1557-3265.sabcs25-gs1-09" count="1">102</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The TROP2-directed ADC datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd) has previously shown a significant PFS benefit, but no OS benefit against chemotherapy of physician’s choice in an HR+/HER2- advanced disease population with progression on 1-2 lines of chemotherapy in the advanced setting and optional prior CDK4/6i exposure (83% of patients) [<citation rid="B103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO.24.00920" pmid="39265124" pmcid="PMC11771365" count="1">103</citation>, <citation rid="B104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.12.017" pmid="41448362" count="1">104</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The TROPION-Breast06 trial is a single-arm phase IIIb trial now evaluating Dato-DXd in advanced HR+/HER2- IHC 0 disease (IHC 0 defined as no staining or incomplete/faint membrane staining in ≤ 10% of tumor cells, reflecting HER2-null or HER2-ultralow status) in chemotherapy-naïve patients after progression on ET [<citation rid="B105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1557-3265.sabcs25-ps5-07-21" count="1">105</citation>, <citation rid="B106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.modpat.2025.100925" pmid="41167529" count="1">106</citation>].

The incorporation of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in addition to chemotherapy-based regimens represents an additional strategy under clinical evaluation. <sentence_start/>The efficacy of ICI therapy in HR+/HER2- breast cancer has been rather disappointing, also reflected in the phase II PACE trial in the post-CDK4/6i setting, in which combining avelumab with palbociclib and fulvestrant failed to improve PFS compared with fulvestrant monotherapy [<citation rid="B56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.23.01940" pmid="38513188" count="1">56</citation>, <citation rid="B107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cancers17172940" pmid="40941037" pmcid="PMC12428055" count="1">107</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Adding pembrolizumab to single-agent chemotherapy is being evaluated in the phase III KEYNOTE-B49 trial in PD-L1-positive patients with prior endocrine and CDK4/6i therapy, but no prior chemotherapy for advanced disease [<citation rid="B108" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2022.40.16_suppl.tps1118" count="1">108</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Preliminary data from the phase II SACI-IO trial (in abstract form) compared SG with or without pembrolizumab after mandatory ET pretreatment and in mostly CDK4/6i- and partially chemotherapy-pretreated patients, and showed no significant PFS benefit at a preliminary analysis. <sentence_start/>Final PFS results are awaited [<citation rid="B109" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.2024.42.17_suppl.lba1004" pmid="42323161" count="1">109</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, the TROP2-directed ADC sacituzumab tirumotecan is currently being evaluated alone and with pembrolizumab vs. chemotherapy in the phase III TroFuse-010 trial in chemotherapy-naïve patients after progression on endocrine and CDK4/6i therapy [<citation rid="B110" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1557-3265.sabcs24-p4-08-09" count="1">110</citation>].

Beyond the therapeutic strategies discussed above, novel agents with alternative mechanisms of action are under investigation, several of which have already progressed to late-phase clinical trials. <sentence_start/>The KAT6 inhibitor PF-07248144 is a novel agent in late clinical development targeting the lysine acetyltransferases KAT6A and KAT6B, which are regulators of chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation [<citation rid="B111" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41523-025-00858-0" pmid="41419492" pmcid="PMC12722229" count="1">111</citation>, <citation rid="B112" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.08.1039" count="1">112</citation>]. <sentence_start/>PF-07248144 is currently being investigated in combination with fulvestrant in the post-CDK4/6i setting in a randomized, phase III trial [<citation rid="B112" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.08.1039" count="1">112</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Other investigative efforts have focused on alternative approaches to CDK inhibition beyond CDK4/6i. <sentence_start/>The more selective CDK4i atirmociclib is under investigation in combination with AI in an advanced first-line setting in phase III trials, directly comparing this approach to the current first-line CDK4/6i standard [<citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.08.1046" count="1">31</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Alternative approaches to target CDKs, such as CDK2 or combined CDK2/4/6 inhibition, and novel PROTACs targeting CDK2 are at earlier stages of clinical development [<citation rid="B113" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41573-026-01431-5" pmid="42045425" count="1">113</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The ADC patritumab deruxtecan, targeting HER3, has shown efficacy in a phase II trial, and is currently also under investigation in a phase III trial in the post CDK4/6i setting [<citation rid="B114" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1557-3265.sabcs25-ps5-07-22" count="1">114</citation>].

Therapeutic decision-making in the second-line setting following CDK4/6i progression is complex, owing to several factors: the rapidly expanding therapeutic landscape with multiple emerging options, the absence of direct head-to-head comparisons between available agents, limited cross-trial comparability, which as such has inherent limitations, but is further complicated in this setting by heterogeneous trial populations that may differentially influence treatment effects, the use of suboptimal comparator treatments, the largely absent mature OS data across available trials, fast changes in the first-line and adjuvant treatment standards with direct implications for subsequent therapy and the temporal and methodological aspects of biomarker assessment. <sentence_start/>In addition, there are unresolved questions of particular complexity, including the management of targetable co-alterations and the question of whether biomarker-selected therapies should be preferred over biomarker-unselected therapies in biomarker-positive patients. <sentence_start/>Treatment selection is therefore guided by general clinical considerations rather than definite evidence-based recommendations. <sentence_start/>An overview of the current treatment options with a potential decision tree reflecting the authors’ opinions is provided in Figure 2 and elaborated in the following section, focused on the most recent results from randomized phase III trial data.

Key considerations in patients progressing on ET and CDK4/6i concern, on the one hand, the need for response, which we define as a function of tumor burden with cancer-related symptoms, risk of organ dysfunction including impending visceral crisis, or imminent tumor-related complications. <sentence_start/>In the presence of a high need for response, prioritizing chemotherapy-based approaches should be considered. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, decision-making depends on the probability of response to a further non-chemotherapy-based strategy (endocrine-based therapy or PARPi), which may be informed by treatment history (pretreatment duration and response, previous CDK4/6i exposure in more than one setting, prior use of targeted agents or SERDs) and biomarker profile. <sentence_start/>In addition, disease kinetics play an important role at both levels of this framework: rapid progression may itself indicate a high need for response, and simultaneously inform the assessment of residual endocrine sensitivity. <sentence_start/>As the general sequencing principle in HR+/HER2- breast cancer favors exhausting ET-based options prior to transitioning to a chemotherapy-based approach [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="B115" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/op-24-00547" pmid="39190846" count="1">115</citation>], a low probability of response does not preclude a further attempt at ET-based therapy in the context of indolent disease.

Biomarker status is central to the subsequent treatment choice, but therapeutic decision-making is informed by additional factors and includes the incorporation of the pretreatment history, including tolerability, duration of response and therapeutic agents used in previous treatment lines, disease burden and kinetics, comorbidities and general health condition of the patient, treatment availability and patient preferences. <sentence_start/>The interplay of these factors ultimately determines the choice between biomarker-guided and biomarker-agnostic strategies. <sentence_start/>Potential therapeutic strategies stratified by biomarker status are shown in Figure 2.

The interdependence and mutual influence of factors outlined above can be illustrated in the case of an <italic>ESR1</italic> detection. <sentence_start/>Three agents have shown efficacy in phase III trials as endocrine monotherapy in <italic>ESR1</italic> mutant disease: elacestrant, imlunestrant and vepdegestrant [<citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.ccr-24-1073" pmid="39087959" pmcid="PMC11443208" count="1">43</citation>, <citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2505725" pmid="40454645" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this context, the exploratory analysis of elacestrant showing an association of pronounced efficacy with longer prior CDK4/6i duration is cited across guidelines and is reflected, for example, in reimbursement criteria in Switzerland, though the post-hoc design necessitates cautious interpretation [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="B116" ref-type="bibr" count="1">116</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Clinical scenarios in which endocrine monotherapy in <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated patients may be favored include a low urgency for tumor response-given the consistently steep initial PFS decline observed across all monotherapy regimens-or concerns regarding tolerability of combination regimens [<citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.ccr-24-1073" pmid="39087959" pmcid="PMC11443208" count="1">43</citation>, <citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2505725" pmid="40454645" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In simple terms, these novel ER targeting agents are an option in patients with <italic>ESR1</italic> mutated disease if 1) achieving tumor stasis rather than regression is sufficient and for 2) low volume disease in which tumor progression does not result in imminent complications such as symptoms and/or organ dysfunction. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, although imlunestrant and abemaciclib showed superiority over imlunestrant in an unselected patient population in terms of PFS (and in an exploratory subgroup analysis irrespective of <italic>ESR1</italic> mutation status), imlunestrant may be preferred over the combination therapy in <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated patients in the clinical scenario outlined above-notably the absence of the need for a rapid tumor response (ORR 11% vs. 29% for imlunestrant vs. the combination therapy in ITT, respectively; and ORR of 12% with imlunestrant for <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated patients in the imlunestrant vs. IC ET arm), poor prior CDK4/6i tolerability; or prior abemaciclib exposure, given the low proportion of abemaciclib-pretreated patients enrolled in the EMBER-3 trial [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The position of everolimus and giredestrant within the treatment landscape-for which abstract-presented data have shown a PFS benefit in the ITT population, and pronounced in the <italic>ESR1</italic>-mutated subgroup (both primary endpoints)-remains to be defined pending full publication of the evERA trial [<citation rid="B50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.09.026" count="1">50</citation>].

For patients with <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated tumors, both alpelisib-fulvestrant and capivasertib-fulvestrant are effective treatment options. <sentence_start/>In the absence of head-to-head comparisons, toxicity profiles become a key treatment-selection criterion. <sentence_start/>The safety profile assessment, based on cross-trial comparison in the absence of head-to-head comparison data, demonstrated higher reporting rates for grade ≥ 3 hyperglycemia with alpelisib than capivasertib (37% and 2.3%), warranting special consideration in patients with pre-existing diabetes mellitus. <sentence_start/>Grade 3 or higher diarrhea and rash differed less markedly between the two regimens (diarrhea rates of 7% and 9%, and rash rates of 10% and 12% for alpelisib and capivasertib, respectively) [<citation rid="B77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2020.11.011" pmid="33246021" count="1">77</citation>, <citation rid="B82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2214131" pmid="37256976" pmcid="PMC11335038" count="1">82</citation>].

A novel feature in treatment selection is the introduction of the absence of a specific mutation-namely <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-WT status-as a biomarker to guide therapy. <sentence_start/>This approach is based on proven efficacy of gedatolisib doublet and triplet combinations in a <italic>PIK3CA-</italic>WT population; although direct comparisons of these treatments are lacking, and gedatolisib has not yet received FDA or EMA approval [<citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>-<citation rid="B88" ref-type="bibr" count="1">88</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Paradoxically, evidence on the use of gedatolisib-based therapies in <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated disease is yet lacking-a gap expected to be addressed by Study 2 of the VIKTORIA-1 trial, which focuses on a <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated population [<citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>].

With respect to <italic>BRCA1/2</italic>-mutated disease, the evidence supporting PARPi use is heterogeneous and requires consideration for treatment selection. <sentence_start/>While PARPi have shown efficacy in patients with <italic>gBRCA1/2</italic> mutations, randomized phase III evidence was not derived from a CDK4/6i-pretreated population. <sentence_start/>Whereas prospective evidence for <italic>sBRCA1/2</italic> and <italic>gPALB2</italic> alterations is derived from mostly CDK4/6i pretreated cohorts (and for olaparib only), it remains confined to studies with limited sample size and ORR as the primary endpoint [<citation rid="B90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.20.02151" pmid="33119476" count="1">90</citation>, <citation rid="B92" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02075" pmid="41604601" count="1">92</citation>].

A biomarker-undefined treatment approach is indicated in the absence of targetable alterations, or if a non-biomarker-guided approach in a biomarker-positive patient is preferred due to clinical or disease-related characteristics.

There are three options to combine a SERD with a CDK4/6i: For fulvestrant-ribociclib and fulvestrant-abemaciclib, treatment effect was demonstrated in populations primarily pretreated with palbociclib. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the benefit following prior exposure to a different CDK4/6i remains unclear [<citation rid="B59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.02392" pmid="37207300" count="1">59</citation>, <citation rid="B60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco-24-02086" pmid="39693591" pmcid="PMC11936477" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the trial evaluating imlunestrant-abemaciclib, only a proportion of patients had received prior CDK4/6 inhibition (predominantly palbociclib), limiting the applicability in the post-CDK4/6i setting [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In an exploratory analysis of fulvestrant-ribociclib-treated patients with evaluable ctDNA in the MAINTAIN trial, patients harboring <italic>ESR1</italic> or <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations had comparable PFS between the fulvestrant-ribociclib and fulvestrant monotherapy arms, whereas the addition of ribociclib appeared beneficial mainly in mutation-negative patients. <sentence_start/>Although based on an exploratory analysis with low patient numbers, the analysis represents an attempt to examine the efficacy of biomarker-undirected therapies in biomarker-positive populations [<citation rid="B59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.02392" pmid="37207300" count="1">59</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For imlunestrant-abemaciclib, a benefit was consistent regardless of <italic>ESR1</italic> mutation or PI3K-AKT pathway status in prespecified exploratory subgroup analyses [<citation rid="B46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2410858" pmid="39660834" count="1">46</citation>, <citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, several therapeutic options still originating from the pre-CDK4/6i era remain available, including ET monotherapy with fulvestrant or everolimus-based regimens [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>], the latter requiring careful consideration of associated toxicities, including hyperglycemia, pneumonitis or stomatitis [<citation rid="B117" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.esmoop.2025.105936" pmid="41604817" pmcid="PMC12865632" count="1">117</citation>].

A further unresolved issue is the optimal prioritization of treatment options in the presence of co-alterations. <sentence_start/>Co-occurrence of <italic>ESR1</italic> and <italic>PIK3CA</italic> for example is consistently reported, with varying prevalence rates [<citation rid="B118" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10549-024-07376-w" pmid="38872062" pmcid="PMC11420341" count="1">118</citation>, <citation rid="B119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.esmoop.2024.103731" pmid="39357123" pmcid="PMC11480226" count="1">119</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The complexity of co-altered disease may be more directly addressed in clinical trials evaluating combination therapies targeting co-occurring alterations, such as oral SERDs and PI3K/AKT/mTOR-pathway directed agents.

If a chemotherapy-based approach is deemed the most appropriate next therapy line, T-DXd represents an effective option for HER2-low disease, particularly due to its comparatively high ORR of 57%, exceeding the ORR reported for single-agent chemotherapy (32%) in the DESTINY-Breast06 trial [<citation rid="B97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa2407086" pmid="39282896" count="1">97</citation>], and-based on cross-trial comparisons-ORRs achieved by endocrine-based combination therapies from current randomized trials in HER2- populations (ORRs 17-32%) [<citation rid="B47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2025.11.018" pmid="41391667" pmcid="PMC13485152" count="1">47</citation>, <citation rid="B59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.02392" pmid="37207300" count="1">59</citation>, <citation rid="B60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco-24-02086" pmid="39693591" pmcid="PMC11936477" count="1">60</citation>, <citation rid="B82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2214131" pmid="37256976" pmcid="PMC11335038" count="1">82</citation>, <citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, pre-existing cardiac insufficiency or pulmonary comorbidities warrant consideration given its potential cardiotoxic effect and the risk of ILD, and OS data for T-DXd in this setting are still lacking [<citation rid="B97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa2407086" pmid="39282896" count="1">97</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The evidence base for the use of T-DXd in HER2-ultralow disease derives from an exploratory, prespecified analysis of the DESTINY-Breast06 trial and based on these data, is listed as treatment option in current guidelines [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="B97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa2407086" pmid="39282896" count="1">97</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Due to the observed intracranial activity of T-DXd in HER2-low tumors, it might be a preferred agent in patients with brain metastases [<citation rid="B99" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2023.09.565" count="1">99</citation>, <citation rid="B100" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.esmoop.2024.103699" pmid="39255534" pmcid="PMC11415677" count="1">100</citation>].

As outlined above, second-line systemic therapy strategies following progression on CDK4/6i have evolved as a biomarker-oriented field, in which therapeutic algorithms incorporate molecular and/or immunohistochemical biomarker testing and one-to-one matching of therapeutic options, which is a consequence of the design from current clinical trials and supports in its simplicity clinical decision making. <sentence_start/>However, clinical utility of a predictive biomarker might be determined by several, often interrelated considerations.

The oncogenic relevance of the currently clinically relevant biomarkers in second-line HR+/HER2- ABC varies: <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations confer ligand-independent ER activation and represent an acquired resistance mechanism arising under AI therapy [<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13058-020-01290-x" pmid="32466779" pmcid="PMC7254698" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/annonc/mdx483" pmid="29045530" pmcid="PMC6264798" count="1">36</citation>]<italic>,</italic> whereas <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations frequently present as early truncal alterations and a pre-treatment oncogenic driver [<citation rid="B64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(23)00676-9" pmid="38547898" count="1">64</citation>, <citation rid="B72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature11412" pmid="23000897" pmcid="PMC3465532" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>HER2-low expression, on the contrary, does not appear to confer relevant oncogenic signal activity in HR+/HER2- breast cancer, but rather serves as a cell-surface target for ADC delivery [<citation rid="B120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-43324-w" pmid="37980405" pmcid="PMC10657399" count="1">120</citation>-<citation rid="B122" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2023.05.008" pmid="37269905" count="1">122</citation>].
Testing strategy: specimen source, testing timepoint and analytical methods

The likelihood of detecting a biomarker in a tissue biopsy is strongly influenced by intrapatient tumor heterogeneity. <sentence_start/>An autopsy study from metastatic breast cancer patients, employing multi-platform profiling on multiregional metastases, demonstrated that clinically actionable driver alterations could be truncal and present across metastases, or confined to a subset of lesions. <sentence_start/>In this study, <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations were detected in two patients and were only present in a subset of metastases, whereas <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations were uniformly detected in all metastases in one patient and in only a subset of metastases in another patient [<citation rid="B123" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2019.04.098" pmid="31141692" pmcid="PMC6546974" count="1">123</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, substantial intrapatient heterogeneity regarding co-existence of low, ultralow and absence of HER2 expression within the same patient, including in metastases within the same organ, have been demonstrated [<citation rid="B124" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.labinv.2025.104202" pmid="40449798" count="1">124</citation>, <citation rid="B125" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ejca.2023.04.026" pmid="37247580" count="1">125</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These observations illustrate that the detection of a biomarker in a single tissue biopsy does not guarantee its functional dominance across the metastatic landscape. <sentence_start/>Also, the absence of biomarker detection in a given lesion does not preclude its presence in other lesions.

In this context, ctDNA-based liquid biopsy might represent a complementary approach with the theoretical advantage of analyzing tumor-derived DNA from multiple metastatic sites. <sentence_start/>However, due to the low concentration of ctDNA in circulation, reliable analysis depends on accurate isolation methods, sensitive assays and careful pre-analytical handling to preserve ctDNA integrity [<citation rid="B126" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jlb.2023.100002" pmid="40027284" pmcid="PMC11863823" count="1">126</citation>].

Studies focusing on concordance rates for <italic>PIK3CA</italic> detection between ctDNA and tissue have reported variable results, possibly due to differences in diagnostic methodology and temporal interval between matched samples. <sentence_start/>In a study of 72 matched tissue and plasma samples analyzed for predefined <italic>PIK3CA</italic> hotspot mutations with multiplexed PCR-based barcoding of DNA, the concordance rate was 72%, with 14% of mutations detected exclusively in plasma and 8% exclusively in tissue; however, the analyzed samples were not always temporally matched [<citation rid="B127" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41416-021-01601-9" pmid="34754095" pmcid="PMC8810831" count="1">127</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In a retrospective cohort of patients with tissue and plasma samples taken the same day, concordance rate for three prespecified <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations was 100% using BEAMing (PCR-based method). <sentence_start/>Importantly, in the prospective cohort with a temporal offset between matched samples (median time between tissue and blood sample: 5 years), the concordance rate was lower (73%) [<citation rid="B128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.ccr-11-2696" pmid="22421194" pmcid="PMC3533370" count="1">128</citation>].

In a recent analysis of a large real-world cohort of breast cancer patients, actionable alterations (including <italic>BRCA1/2, ESR1</italic> and <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations) were assessed by next-generation sequencing (NGS) in temporally matched ctDNA and tissue samples. <sentence_start/>Approximately 59% of alterations were concordantly detected by both modalities, whereas approximately 20% of alterations were identified exclusively by ctDNA, and 21% by tissue profiling. <sentence_start/>The concordance rates varied between genes; and <italic>PIK3CA</italic> demonstrated the highest concordance (70%) between tissue and ctDNA. <sentence_start/>For <italic>ESR1</italic>, 65% of variants detected by only one modality were found exclusively by ctDNA [<citation rid="B129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.51700" pmid="38252441" pmcid="PMC10804266" count="1">129</citation>].

As an additional level of complexity, reliable biomarker detection is contingent not only on the specimen type, but also the timing of testing. <sentence_start/>Due to the dynamic evolution of <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations under selective pressure of AI [<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13058-021-01462-3" pmid="34392831" pmcid="PMC8365900" count="1">34</citation>], testing is indicated on a current sample reflecting post-ET progression status. <sentence_start/>For <italic>PIK3CA</italic>, mostly considered an early truncal alteration, a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of real-world genomic profiling data from HR+/HER2- breast cancer suggested a relatively stable prevalence of <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations at successive lines of therapy in tissue biopsies [<citation rid="B118" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10549-024-07376-w" pmid="38872062" pmcid="PMC11420341" count="1">118</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the AURORA program, prospective genomic profiling demonstrated that <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations were enriched in metastases compared to their paired primary tumors in mostly treatment-naïve patients, or patients treated with up to one prior line of therapy; however, in the HR+/HER2- subcohort, the rate of <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations private to metastasis was low [<citation rid="B71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.cd-20-1647" pmid="34183353" pmcid="PMC9414283" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, serial ctDNA sequencing from the PALOMA-3 trial (fulvestrant and palbociclib vs. fulvestrant in an endocrine-resistant population) demonstrated an increase in <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutation prevalence during treatment. <sentence_start/>Of the presumably acquired mutations, 33% were detected at low allele frequencies at baseline by droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), suggesting selection of pre-existing subclones alongside treatment-related acquisition of new mutations [<citation rid="B73" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.cd-18-0264" pmid="30206110" pmcid="PMC6368247" count="1">73</citation>].

Biomarker detection is further influenced by technical and methodological differences among diagnostic assays, including the spectrum of alterations covered and the underlying detection technology. <sentence_start/>In SOLAR-1 and the VIKTORIA-1 trial, <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutation status was determined using a PCR test covering predefined hotspot mutations (Table 3) [<citation rid="B76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa1813904" pmid="31091374" count="1">76</citation>, <citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, studies with real-world genomic profiling and aggregated genomic datasets suggest that ≥ 20% of pathogenic <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutations in ABC are not captured by the SOLAR-1 panel, including <italic>N345K</italic>, which might occur more frequently than some included variants [<citation rid="B74" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13058-020-01284-9" pmid="32404150" pmcid="PMC7222307" count="1">74</citation>, <citation rid="B130" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.ccr-22-2115" pmid="36321996" pmcid="PMC10011882" count="1">130</citation>].

Similarly, different diagnostic approaches for <italic>ESR1</italic> mutation detection are applied across recent studies. <sentence_start/>In PADA-1, ddPCR provides high sensitivity for hotspot mutations; however, despite covering the majority of actionable mutations, it remains restricted to predefined variants (Table 3) [<citation rid="B57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1470-2045(22)00555-1" pmid="36183733" count="1">57</citation>, <citation rid="B131" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2023.102642" pmid="37864956" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, NGS-based approaches, as applied in SERENA-6 and EMERALD, enable broader detection of <italic>ESR1</italic> variants [<citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.00338" pmid="35584336" pmcid="PMC9553388" count="1">41</citation>, <citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2502929" pmid="40454637" count="1">45</citation>, <citation rid="B131" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ctrv.2023.102642" pmid="37864956" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These methodological differences can influence the classification of patients as biomarker-positive or -negative, and for <italic>ESR1,</italic> have become particularly relevant when the biomarker serves as marker defining molecular progression prompting a treatment switch [<citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2502929" pmid="40454637" count="1">45</citation>, <citation rid="B57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S1470-2045(22)00555-1" pmid="36183733" count="1">57</citation>].

The predictive value of a biomarker and its implementation in clinical decision-making is ultimately determined by evidence derived from clinical trials. <sentence_start/>Several methodological aspects regarding biomarker-analysis at the trial-design level may potentially influence observed treatment effects with respect to biomarker-defined subgroups. <sentence_start/>Patients with unevaluable biomarker status can be classified as biomarker-negative, with inconsistent reporting across studies, randomization stratification according to biomarker status can vary, and diagnostic assays differ (Table 3). <sentence_start/>The definition and assessment of a molecularly defined subgroup can influence the treatment effect in a biomarker-selected subgroup, which was illustrated by the phase II FAKTION trial. <sentence_start/>Capivasertib plus fulvestrant in AI-resistant disease initially showed benefit over fulvestrant in ITT; with similar effect sizes observed irrespective of PI3K-AKT pathway alteration status (including <italic>PIK3CA</italic> and <italic>PTEN</italic> alterations). <sentence_start/>However, refined post-hoc biomarker analysis using an extended set of molecular alterations (including <italic>AKT1</italic>), and more sensitive diagnostic assays, resulted in substantial patient reclassification. <sentence_start/>The new analysis suggested that clinical benefit was confined to pathway-altered tumors, with no signal of efficacy observed in biomarker-negative disease, underscoring the importance of precise molecular stratification [<citation rid="B132" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(19)30817-4" pmid="32035020" pmcid="PMC7052734" count="1">132</citation>, <citation rid="B133" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1470-2045(22)00284-4" pmid="35671774" pmcid="PMC9630162" count="1">133</citation>].

In addition, some phase III clinical trials investigating treatment effects according to biomarker status incorporate a dual-testing framework comprising a biomarker-unselected and a biomarker-selected population. <sentence_start/>Biomarker-negative populations are then investigated in an exploratory setting, which may reduce the likelihood of detecting treatment effects in this subgroup.

Study 1 of the two-part VIKTORIA-1 trial takes a novel, methodologically distinct approach by assessing treatment efficacy in a specifically mutation-negative population: The PI3K/mTORC1/2 inhibitor gedatolisib has demonstrated activity in an exclusively <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-WT population, providing more robust evidence especially for patients without actionable alterations [<citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>]. <sentence_start/>As gedatolisib additionally functions as an mTORC inhibitor, the observed treatment effect may be mediated through mTOR inhibition, which acts downstream of PI3K and for which patient selection has not been biomarker-driven [<citation rid="B86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO-25-02643" pmid="41802242" pmcid="PMC13075786" count="1">86</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In study 2 of VIKTORIA-1, focusing on the <italic>PIK3CA</italic>-mutated cohort, the gedatolisib combination therapies will be compared to alpelisib and fulvestrant and will provide further insights into the clinical significance of <italic>PIK3CA</italic> with respect to gedatolisib activity [<citation rid="B134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1538-7445.sabcs23-po2-20-02" count="1">134</citation>].

The evolving understanding of the predictive value of biomarkers is illustrated by T-DXd and HER2 expression; initially restricted to HER2-positive patients [<citation rid="B135" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2115022" pmid="35320644" count="1">135</citation>], it has also shown clinically relevant efficacy in HER2-low disease and has shown signals of activity even in HER2-ultralow tumors [<citation rid="B97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa2407086" pmid="39282896" count="1">97</citation>].

Due to the spatial and temporal heterogeneity, and variability in analytical methods, recommendations for the assessment of biomarkers in clinical practice differ between individual biomarkers. <sentence_start/>Regarding <italic>PIK3CA</italic>, <italic>AKT1</italic> and <italic>PTEN</italic> testing, current guidelines either mostly do not address whether ctDNA or tissue should be preferred, or list both options without hierarchy. <sentence_start/>Similarly, no clear preference is established with respect to timing (archival vs. current sample) or lesion type (primary vs. metastatic site) [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="B136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/JCO.24.00248" pmid="38478799" count="1">136</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Of note, NCCN Guidelines<sup>®</sup> recommend to prefer tissue-based testing over ctDNA to detect <italic>PTEN</italic> homozygous copy loss [<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Today, <italic>PIK3CA</italic> mutation status is the only biomarker required already before the start of a first-line palliative therapy in case of recurrence during or shortly after adjuvant ET based on the results of the INAVO120 trial [<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2501796" pmid="40454641" pmcid="PMC13496148" count="1">26</citation>]. <sentence_start/>With respect to <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations, given the dynamic acquisition of <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations under ET, current guidelines recommend testing for <italic>ESR1</italic> at time of progression on ET, preferably with ctDNA or, alternatively, within a tumor tissue sample [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="B137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.23.00638" pmid="37196213" count="1">137</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the determination of HER2-low status is IHC-based and thus only assessable in tissue. <sentence_start/>Guidelines acknowledge the temporal and spatial heterogeneity of HER2 expression and recommend a repeat biopsy or the integration of results from all available prior and concurrent samples, where this may inform clinical decision-making [<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2026.05.707" pmid="42217581" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="B138" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/jco.22.02864" pmid="37284804" count="1">138</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Regarding diagnostic assays, the ESMO Precision Medicine Working group advocated 2024 for NGS as SOC; however, this recommendation predates the introduction of inavolisib in the first-line palliative therapy; and does not account for the divergent timepoints of the disease course at which <italic>PIK3CA</italic> and <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations are required [<citation rid="B139" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.annonc.2024.04.005" pmid="38834388" count="1">139</citation>].

In summary, in the post-CDK4/6i setting, the highlighted multifaceted variables of therapeutically actionable biomarkers ask for a personalized strategy on a case-to-case basis, but in general requires the determination of predictive biomarkers on a freshly obtained blood (ctDNA) or tissue sample, due to the acquisition of <italic>ESR1</italic> mutations during ET. <sentence_start/>As a rule of thumb, we favor ctDNA testing in cases of difficult-to-access lesions or widespread tumor progression. <sentence_start/>A fresh tissue biopsy could be considered suitable in cases of isolated progression (with the goal to capture the molecular landscape of the progressive lesion); and/or when a switch to a chemotherapy-based regimen is clinically indicated and prior HER2 assessments have indicated HER2-null status (IHC 0 with complete absence of membrane staining, thus not meeting the criteria for HER2-ultralow) [<citation rid="B106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.modpat.2025.100925" pmid="41167529" count="1">106</citation>].

The treatment landscape of HR+/HER2- ABC in the post-CDK4/6i setting has become increasingly complex, with a growing number of therapeutic options but no standardized treatment algorithms. <sentence_start/>Treatment selection therefore requires an individualized approach integrating patient- and disease-related factors. <sentence_start/>While biomarker-guided strategies are central to guide treatment decisions, their optimal clinical implementation requires careful evaluation of their biological, contextual and methodological complexity.

The prevailing singular biomarker-driven approach appears insufficient to fully capture context-dependent disease biology and its associated heterogeneity in treatment response. <sentence_start/>With the fast pace of emerging new therapies, it becomes increasingly difficult to design clinical trials focusing on unmet needs, such as therapy sequencing or prioritizing of biomarker-uninformed vs. -informed approaches, which are still of clinical value at completion. <sentence_start/>There is a need for a more holistic profiling strategy that accounts for individual disease biology and enables the prediction of therapeutic susceptibility in different clinical scenarios.

A suggested strategy is represented by precision oncology focused trials using multi-omics profiling and functional drug screening [<citation rid="B140" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1557-3265.sabcs25-ps5-07-18" count="1">140</citation>] resulting in patient allocation to clearly predefined treatment strategies. <sentence_start/>Along these lines, the LINUX trial pioneered this approach with reclassification of HR+/HER2- breast cancer using a multi-omics approach, translation of these classifications into artificial intelligence-assisted digital pathology methods and as a result, patient allocation to different treatment arms [<citation rid="B141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2025.11.003" pmid="41349543" count="1">141</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Complementary to these efforts, a deeper mechanistic understanding of sensitivity and resistance to ET-based treatment strategies may be advanced through cutting-edge translational research programs accompanying clinical trials with patient avatars (patient-derived xenograft or organoid models) to model treatment resistance and repeat biopsies upon disease progression for transcriptomic, genomic and (phospho)proteomic analysis, followed by functional assays to validate the causality of the obtained correlative results. <sentence_start/>Collaboration between research laboratories and oncologists should be fostered to ensure that mechanistic research remains responsive to emerging developments and unmet needs in medical oncology. <sentence_start/>In the context of unresolved clinical questions, existing real-world data containing available molecular tumor profiles hold substantial potential for hypothesis-generating findings regarding, e.g., therapy sequencing and association of therapy response with somatic molecular alterations beyond those covered in clinical trials.

Clinical practice is shaped by phase III trial results and depends on trial design allowing for successful translation into routine care. <sentence_start/>Benefits in PFS observed in clinical trials have constituted the predominant measure of efficacy of investigated treatment strategies. <sentence_start/>Demonstration of OS benefit is hampered by the requirement for prolonged follow-up and possible inherent dilution effect imposed by the continuously changing treatment landscape and subsequent treatment lines. <sentence_start/>Given these limitations, the incorporation of patient-centered and/or patient-defined endpoints into trial design assumes increasing importance, such as health-related quality of life or preservation of functional independence.
